solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Boris's upset with cut – "time to replace one's hamper"

indicators.note: one thing taking the place of another means a letter is swapped out for a new letter
something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time
I is the Roman numeral one, the letter thrown out

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson is upset about a spending cut and a complaint about his hamper of food.
explanation.walkthrough: BORIS plus CUT has the right letters except an I where a T should be; swap that one for time and jumble the result. 'Boris's' reads as 'Boris is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To hamper someone is to get in their way, so the verb is a straightforward synonym meaning impede or block progress.

clue.text: The management's pissed off broadcast

indicators.note: something broadcast goes out over the airwaves, so we hear the word rather than read it

blocks.note: being bored is being fed up, a milder form of pissed off

explanation.surface: Bosses are fed up with a radio or TV programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed off' here means fed up, which is a sense of bored rather than angry; the sound of that word gives the spelling for the company directors.
explanation.definitionFit: A company's board of directors runs it, so the collective noun names the people in charge of a business.

clue.text: Such as Billy Elliot's nasty e-troll in neckwear

indicators.note: something nasty is twisted and spoiled, so these letters are mangled into a new order
one thing placed in another sits inside it, so the word goes within the outer letters

blocks.note: a tie is worn around the neck
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spiteful online troll attacks Billy Elliot while wearing a tie.
explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled troll letters sit between TI and E of the tie. Billy Elliot is a film and musical named after its lead character.
explanation.definitionFit: The part named in a work's own name is that work's lead, and Billy Elliot is both the show and its hero, an example of this.

clue.text: New in this country, present name 'alien'

indicators.note: something placed in another lands inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the setter's country is the United Kingdom
N is the abbreviation for new
the present is now
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A recent arrival in Britain is presented with the label 'alien'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' looks like an adjective describing an immigrant, but it is just the abbreviation, placed inside 'this country'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something alien is strange and unfamiliar to us, which is what unfamiliar or unrecognised things are called.

clue.text: X might represent this organ

blocks.note: first meaning: the multiplication sign in arithmetic
second meaning: a newspaper

explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' wants to be a body part; in crosswords it often means a newspaper, the mouthpiece of some body or party.
explanation.definitionFit: The cross sign is read aloud as multiplied by in sums, and the London daily paper is a classic news publication.

clue.text: Building a party space back-to-front

indicators.note: facing back-to-front means running the wrong way, so the letters are read in reverse order

blocks.note: taken as written
a do is a party
a gap is a space

explanation.surface: Constructing a venue for a party with the room laid out the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back-to-front' reverses the whole string A, DO, GAP, not just the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiered tower is a temple structure in East Asia, so it is a specific example of an edifice.

clue.text: Split pea inserted in member is a barrier

indicators.note: something split is broken apart, letting its letters fall into a new order
inserting means putting inside, so one word goes within another

blocks.note: a member is a part of a whole, as a limb is of a body
taken as written

explanation.surface: Split peas lodged in someone's body form an obstruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' wants to be a limb or club member; here it is simply a part of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A low protective wall along a roof edge or bridge stops people falling, a kind of guard wall or screen.

clue.text: Gusset mangled – time to go for work out

indicators.note: when something has to go it leaves, so that letter is dropped
something mangled is crushed out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word minus its T, the time abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone's underwear gusset got wrecked during a workout at the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work out' reads as gym exercise; it is the definition, meaning to figure out. A gusset is a reinforcing panel in clothing such as tights or pants.
explanation.definitionFit: To work out an answer is to reach it by reasoning, and making an estimate or conjecture is a loose sense of that.

clue.text: Democrat coalition dawdling

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for Democrat
a coalition is an alliance

explanation.surface: A Democratic coalition is dragging its feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dawdling' is read as a noun here, the act of lingering, to match the noun answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Dalliance can mean idle time-wasting or loitering, so as a noun it matches dawdling used as a gerund.

clue.text: Time right after strip for a noted man

blocks.note: a bar is a strip, as of metal
T is the abbreviation for time
OK means all right

explanation.surface: It's time for a man to strip for a famous man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' looks like famous but means dealing in musical notes; Béla Bartók was a Hungarian composer.
explanation.definitionFit: A man of musical notes is the crossword's playful way of describing a composer, here a celebrated twentieth-century one.

clue.text: Boris's retreat upset Drive magazine

indicators.note: in a down-reading sense, upset means turned over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to ram is to drive in hard
Bella is a British women's weekly magazine

explanation.surface: Boris's holiday retreat annoyed a motoring magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive magazine' looks like one title; Drive gives RAM, turned round, and Bella is a separate magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Marbella is a Spanish resort on the Costa del Sol where Boris Johnson took a holiday, so it serves as his getaway spot.

clue.text: Loose talk not working? Go and piss off!

indicators.note: something gone off is out of order, so its letters are disturbed into a new sequence

blocks.note: idle means not working
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone fed up with the chatter of slackers tells them to get lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piss off' reads as a rude dismissal, but 'off' only scrambles the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose talk is careless chatter, and the phrase means rumour-mongering or chit-chat without basis.

clue.text: see 21ac.
Seize one's money

blocks.note: one is I, and 'one's' is read as 'one is', I'M
the pound is British money

explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' looks possessive, but it stands for 'one is', which becomes I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: To impound property, such as a car, is to take legal custody of it, so it means confiscate.

clue.text: Barely perceptible hand gesture, but it should heat things up

blocks.note: micro means tiny
a wave is a gesture of the hand

explanation.surface: A tiny flirtatious signal of the hand might still get things going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heat things up' sounds like sexual tension; it is the kitchen oven.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen appliance whose job is warming food, so the definition describes its purpose cryptically.

clue.text: Blokes only popular with money, putting on a show

blocks.note: a stag party or night is for men only
in means fashionable, popular
G is a grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: Men-only clubs welcoming the rich are showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: A stag night is a British bachelor party, so 'stag' means males only.
explanation.definitionFit: Staging a play is mounting a production of it in a theatre, the same as presenting a performance.

clue.text: Again I let out member and companions?

indicators.note: letting something out frees it from its order, so the letters are free to be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man confesses he has again let his privates out, along with his friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' and 'companions' read as people in a club; the member is the penis and its companions the rest of the private parts.
explanation.definitionFit: The penis plus its neighbouring parts make up the external sex organs, a cheeky way of describing the whole set.

clue.text: Finished after sexual partner's disaster

blocks.note: a screw is slang for a sex partner
time is up when it is finished

explanation.surface: A relationship is over and the lover regards it as a catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sexual partner's' reads as possessive, but the 's is just 'is' linking wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A screw-up is a bungled mess, so informally it means a blunder or fiasco.

clue.text: Never a loser, bishop escapes – not put away

indicators.note: whatever escapes gets away and is no longer there, so that letter goes

blocks.note: one never defeated is unbeaten
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: An undefeated bishop gets away and isn't locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' sounds like prison, but it means food eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting food away is informal for eating it, so food not put away remains on the plate untouched.

clue.text: Second fiddle – arsehole

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
to fiddle with something is to tinker

explanation.surface: Someone playing second fiddle is called a nasty name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second fiddle' looks like a set phrase, but it splits into S and a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang insults for a contemptible, unpleasant person, so an obnoxious individual is either.

clue.text: Try a bit of sexual stimulation to improve the picture?

definitions.text: Try a bit of sexual stimulation

blocks.clueFragment: Try a bit of sexual stimulation
blocks.note: first meaning: grope or fondle someone
second meaning: retouch a photo or painting

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a single bawdy suggestion; the two halves are separate senses of one phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both groping someone sexually and making small corrections to an image such as a photograph.

clue.text: (& 12ac.) Revered silence before sex that's amazing

blocks.note: something holy is revered
sh is a call for silence
it is slang for sex

explanation.surface: A reverent hush before lovemaking, and then astonishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' as slang for sex is an old crossword favourite, as in 'doing it'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a vulgar exclamation of astonishment, the crude equivalent of saying wow.

clue.text: Tory ultimately lied about supply

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept
turned about means moved around, so the letters are shuffled

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician in the end lied about supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning'; it jumbles the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to produce or provide, as a field gives a crop, so it means furnish or provide.

clue.text: A good clear-out gone awry – caution, have to remove top

indicators.note: taking off the top of a word removes its first letter
something gone awry has gone wrong and out of order, so the letters are reshuffled

blocks.note: taken as written
the word with its first letter taken off

explanation.surface: A thorough spring-clean has gone wrong, with a warning to take off the lid.
explanation.walkthrough: A good clear-out is also a toilet joke: emptying the bowels is a meaning of the answer, as well as clearing a building.
explanation.definitionFit: Evacuation means emptying a place of people, or the bowels of their contents, so either is a thorough clearing.

clue.text: Where you'll find racy types like bed

blocks.note: as means like
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: Raunchy people are found in bed, it suggests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racy types' sounds like libertines, but means racegoers: Ascot is the English racecourse famous for Royal Ascot.
explanation.definitionFit: The Berkshire racecourse is a place full of race-goers, punning on racy as fond of horse races.

clue.text: It stands out quite transparently: Boris is extremely lacking, with negative, evil ends

indicators.note: lacking the extremes means without the outermost letters, so only the middle stays
the ends of words are their last letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: the word without its first and last letters
final letter
final letter

explanation.surface: Boris is obviously lacking in substance, being negative with evil ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ends' applies to both 'negative' and 'evil'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oriel is a bay window projecting from an upper storey, so it juts from the wall and is made of glass.

clue.text: Like Brenda's one joke captured by sound device

indicators.note: something captured is held by its captor, so it sits inside the other word

blocks.note: a mic is a microphone
a means one
a jest is a joke

explanation.surface: One of Brenda's jokes is picked up on a microphone.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, so 'Like Brenda's' means like Her Majesty's.
explanation.definitionFit: Majestic means regal and stately, the quality belonging to a monarch, so it describes the Queen's manner.

clue.text: Hang on – have in one's power one Tory leader!

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: to hold is to have in one's control
I is the Roman numeral one
first letter

explanation.surface: Wait – someone has the Conservative leader at their mercy!
explanation.walkthrough: Tory leader is the first letter of Tory, a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations asking someone to wait or stop for a moment, so they are interchangeable commands.

clue.text: Blunt's deed, an abomination

indicators.note: an abomination is a hideous distortion, so the letters are deformed into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Anthony Blunt, the Soviet spy, committed a monstrous act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blunt' with a capital reads as a person; here it is a verb, to make less sharp. Anthony Blunt was the art historian exposed as a Soviet spy.
explanation.definitionFit: To deaden a sound or feeling is to dull it, which is the verb sense of making something less sharp.

clue.text: Summit on board, where important consumers gather

blocks.note: a summit is the top
a board is a table, as in board and lodging

explanation.surface: A summit meeting with the company board, where the big shoppers meet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consumers' sounds like shoppers; it means diners, who consume food.
explanation.definitionFit: At a formal dinner or wedding, the guests of honour sit at the head table, so it is where VIP diners eat.
